title: The Wholistic Productivity Podcast
author: Chris LeBrun
description: A weekly podcast redefining productivity by ditching the toxic "work harder" mentality in favor of smarter strategies for time management, goal-setting, and professional, personal, and purpose-driven objectives.

episodes.title: #73 | Why Asking for Help Isn't Weakness (Lessons from Who Not How)
episodes.summary: Chris explores why asking for help isn't failure, drawing on his grandfathers' farming community and the book Who Not How to show how hiring expertise saves time and supports professional, personal, and purpose-driven goals.

episodes.title: #72 | The Weekly Review Habit That Stops Bad Weeks From Piling Up
episodes.summary: A simple three-question weekly review that takes under ten minutes, plus Jeff Bezos' regret minimization framework and three ways to close the gap between the moment and the response you wish you'd given.

episodes.title: #71 | Why You Don't Have to Chase Your Goals Alone
episodes.summary: Chris discusses building goals with partners, telling reservations apart from cowardice, and how community accelerates progress, with a nod to Marcus Aurelius and stoic philosophy.

episodes.title: #70 | Decision Fatigue Is Real: Batch Your Choices, Protect Your Focus
episodes.summary: How batching decisions preserves mental energy for the choices that matter. Chris shares his own routines, including the same breakfast every day, weekend meal prep, a two-outfit Friday system, and batching self-care.

episodes.title: #69 | Stop Framing Your Values. Start Using Them
episodes.summary: The difference between values you believe in and values you operate from, with a story about a four-day workweek Chris didn't realize he valued until he reverse-engineered his goals.

episodes.title: #68 | The Not-to-Do List: Stop Doing What's Holding You Back
episodes.summary: An introduction to the not-to-do list as a complement to traditional planning: identify the habits and expectations blocking progress and let them go on purpose.

articles.question: How do you reduce decision fatigue?
articles.metaDescription: Chris LeBrun of The Wholistic Productivity Podcast on reducing decision fatigue by batching small choices so your focus is saved for what counts.
articles.intro: You reduce decision fatigue by making fewer decisions, not by making them faster. On The Wholistic Productivity Podcast, host Chris LeBrun explains that every choice, from what to eat for breakfast to whether to change careers, draws from the same limited well of mental energy. His fix is batching: decide once, in advance, for the small stuff, so you have something left for the big stuff.

sections.heading: Your brain doesn't rank your choices for you
sections.body:
The core idea in the episode is uncomfortable but useful. Your brain does not sort decisions by importance. Picking a shirt, choosing lunch, deciding whether to answer that email now or later, all of it pulls from the same pool of mental energy as the decisions that actually shape your life.

That's why you can feel wiped out at 3 p.m. without having done anything hard. You've spent the morning making dozens of tiny calls, and by the time a real question shows up, the tank is low.

Chris calls this decision fatigue, and he's blunt that it's real. It quietly drains your best thinking before you get to the choices that matter. The goal of the episode isn't to make you tougher. It's to stop you from wasting the energy in the first place.

quote.text: Your brain does not know the difference between deciding what to eat for breakfast and deciding whether to change careers.
quote.speaker: Chris LeBrun

sections.heading: Batching: decide once, repeat all week
sections.body:
Batching means grouping a category of decisions and making them all at once, ahead of time. Instead of asking "what's for dinner?" seven nights in a row, you answer it once on Sunday. Instead of standing in front of the closet every morning, you settle it the night before, or build a rotation you don't have to think about.

Chris walks through his own examples. He eats the same breakfast every day. He preps meals on the weekend. He has what he calls a two-outfit Friday system, which he jokes about as #FlannelFriday. He batches content creation, too, so he's not deciding what to write or record every single day.

None of these are dramatic. That's the point. Each one removes a small, recurring drain, and the drains add up. The episode's chapter list puts the practical section at around the three-minute mark, and it's the part worth replaying if you want to copy his setup.

sections.heading: Building batching into your process instead of your willpower
sections.body:
A one-time batching session helps for a week. To make it stick, Chris suggests making batch decisions part of your regular process rather than something you remember to do when you're already overwhelmed.

In practice that looks like a standing time slot. Meal decisions happen on the weekend. Outfit decisions happen the night before or on a fixed weekly rotation. Content or work-planning decisions happen in one sitting rather than scattered across the week.

The question to ask about any recurring choice is simple: could I decide this once instead of every time? If the answer is yes, it belongs in a batch. You'll be surprised how many of your daily decisions qualify once you start looking.

sections.heading: Self-care is the first thing to batch, not the last
sections.body:
The part of the episode people tend to skip is the section on batching self-care. Chris argues that the decisions around rest, exercise, and connection deserve the same treatment as work decisions. If you leave them to in-the-moment willpower, they lose to whatever is urgent.

So he pre-decides those too. When does the workout happen? When do you call the people who matter to you? Those go on the calendar in batches, the same way meal prep does, so they don't get renegotiated every day when your energy is lowest.

His framing is that self-care isn't a break from productivity. It's what makes the productive hours possible. Batch it, protect it, and you'll notice the big decisions get easier because you're not making them exhausted.

quote.text: Self-care is not a break from productivity, it is the foundation of it.
quote.speaker: Chris LeBrun

keyTakeaways: Every decision, big or small, draws from the same limited pool of mental energy.
Batch recurring choices like meals and outfits so you decide once instead of daily.
Make batching a scheduled part of your week, not something you do when you're already drained.
Batch self-care decisions too, so rest and exercise don't lose to whatever feels urgent.
Fewer small decisions leaves more focus for the choices that actually matter.

faq.q: What are the signs of decision fatigue?
faq.a: Chris describes it as your best thinking draining away before you reach the choices that matter. If you feel mentally spent by mid-afternoon without doing anything demanding, small decisions are probably the culprit.

faq.q: Does eating the same breakfast every day really help?
faq.a: It's one of Chris's own habits. The value isn't the food, it's removing one decision from every morning. Meal prep and a fixed outfit rotation work the same way.

faq.q: How often should I batch decisions?
faq.a: Chris builds it into a regular process, with meal prep on weekends and other choices settled in one sitting rather than scattered through the week. A weekly rhythm is the easiest place to start.

articles.sourceNote: Based on The Wholistic Productivity Podcast episode "#70 | Decision Fatigue Is Real: Batch Your Choices, Protect Your Focus," released July 28, 2026, hosted by Chris LeBrun.
